questions.stem: A 3-year-old with these findings — a brown macule (cafe-au-lait spot) on the trunk and a malformed thumb — together with pancytopenia most likely has which condition?

explanation.summary: Cafe-au-lait spots with skin hypopigmentation, short stature, and radial/thumb anomalies accompanying progressive pancytopenia are classic for Fanconi anemia, an autosomal recessive DNA-repair defect that causes inherited bone marrow failure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cafe-au-lait spots with skin hypopigmentation, short stature, and radial/thumb anomalies accompanying progressive pancytopenia are classic for Fanconi anemia, an autosomal recessive DNA-repair defect that causes inherited bone marrow failure.

questions.stem: This schematic maps the differentiation of a single precursor into all blood cell types. In aplastic anemia the marrow defect shown here spares one branch relatively — cells of which lineage are LEAST reduced?

explanation.summary: Aplastic anemia is caused by loss of myeloid hematopoietic stem cells, so RBCs, platelets, granulocytes, and monocytes all fall (pancytopenia). Lymphoid progenitors arise from a separate branch of this scheme and are relatively preserved, so lymphocyte counts remain near normal on a CBC.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aplastic anemia is caused by loss of myeloid hematopoietic stem cells, so RBCs, platelets, granulocytes, and monocytes all fall (pancytopenia). Lymphoid progenitors arise from a separate branch of this scheme and are relatively preserved, so lymphocyte counts remain near normal on a CBC.

questions.stem: In the experiment shown, the abnormal cells rupture much more readily than normal red cells when placed in the hypotonic solution. What property accounts for their heightened susceptibility to lysis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They lack membrane reserve, so they cannot accommodate water influx before bursting

choices.label: B
choices.text: Membrane-bound antibody makes their lipid bilayer intrinsically fragile

choices.label: C
choices.text: They contain unstable hemoglobin that precipitates and ruptures the cell on swelling

choices.label: D
choices.text: Their high surface-area-to-volume ratio accelerates osmotic water entry

choices.label: E
choices.text: Their sodium-potassium pumps actively pull additional water into the cell

explanation.summary: This is the osmotic fragility test. Normal biconcave cells have excess membrane and can swell to absorb water; spherocytes have little membrane reserve, so even modest water influx in a hypotonic solution causes them to lyse, giving increased osmotic fragility.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is the osmotic fragility test. Normal biconcave cells have excess membrane and can swell to absorb water; spherocytes have little membrane reserve, so even modest water influx in a hypotonic solution causes them to lyse, giving increased osmotic fragility.

questions.stem: This peripheral blood smear shows numerous red cells with an abnormal elongated, cigar-like shape. Which inherited red-cell membrane disorder does this finding most strongly suggest?

explanation.summary: Large numbers of elliptical (oval, cigar-shaped) red cells on a peripheral smear are the hallmark of hereditary elliptocytosis, an autosomal dominant defect commonly involving spectrin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Large numbers of elliptical (oval, cigar-shaped) red cells on a peripheral smear are the hallmark of hereditary elliptocytosis, an autosomal dominant defect commonly involving spectrin.

questions.stem: This peripheral smear shows markedly fragmented red cells of widely varying size and shape, resembling the appearance seen in patients with extensive burns. Which disorder does this represent?

explanation.summary: Hereditary pyropoikilocytosis, caused by two hereditary elliptocytosis mutations, produces striking red-cell fragmentation and bizarre poikilocytes that resemble the burned red cells seen after severe thermal injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hereditary pyropoikilocytosis, caused by two hereditary elliptocytosis mutations, produces striking red-cell fragmentation and bizarre poikilocytes that resemble the burned red cells seen after severe thermal injury.

questions.stem: Compared with the cells on the left, the cells on the right have lost the shape that normally lets red cells deform. What is the main clinical consequence of this altered morphology?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A marked reduction in the oxygen-carrying capacity of each cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failure to be recognized and cleared by the reticuloendothelial system

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased entrapment and destruction within the splenic sinusoids

choices.label: D
choices.text: Widespread intravascular hemolysis within small capillaries

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of the ability to bind and consume haptoglobin

explanation.summary: The rounded cells on the right (spherocytes) lack the membrane excess that allows normal biconcave cells to squeeze through splenic sinusoids, so they are trapped and destroyed there, producing extravascular hemolysis. Their oxygen-carrying capacity remains essentially normal.
explanation.whyCorrect: The rounded cells on the right (spherocytes) lack the membrane excess that allows normal biconcave cells to squeeze through splenic sinusoids, so they are trapped and destroyed there, producing extravascular hemolysis. Their oxygen-carrying capacity remains essentially normal.

questions.stem: The small, round, deeply basophilic inclusions within several red cells on this smear are which structures, and their persistence indicates what functional state?

explanation.summary: Howell-Jolly bodies are nuclear DNA remnants normally removed by a functioning spleen. Their presence signals the absent or non-functioning spleen (functional asplenia) seen in sickle cell disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Howell-Jolly bodies are nuclear DNA remnants normally removed by a functioning spleen. Their presence signals the absent or non-functioning spleen (functional asplenia) seen in sickle cell disease.

questions.stem: On this cellulose acetate gel, hemoglobin variants migrate to different positions. HbS is separated from normal HbA primarily because of a difference in what property?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron content of the heme groups

explanation.summary: The glutamate-to-valine substitution removes a negative charge, so HbS migrates less far toward the anode than HbA in an electric field. Electrophoresis therefore separates hemoglobins mainly by charge.
explanation.whyCorrect: The glutamate-to-valine substitution removes a negative charge, so HbS migrates less far toward the anode than HbA in an electric field. Electrophoresis therefore separates hemoglobins mainly by charge.

questions.stem: This illustration of rigid sickled cells lodged within a small blood vessel depicts the mechanism underlying which major consequence of sickle cell disease?

explanation.summary: Sickled cells lose flexibility and become trapped in capillaries, blocking blood flow. The resulting ischemia and infarction of downstream tissue is termed vaso-occlusive disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sickled cells lose flexibility and become trapped in capillaries, blocking blood flow. The resulting ischemia and infarction of downstream tissue is termed vaso-occlusive disease.

questions.stem: In this schematic, HbS molecules aggregate into long strands when blood becomes deoxygenated, distorting the cell. What molecular process deforms the red blood cell into a sickle shape?

explanation.summary: In the taut, deoxygenated state the exposed hydrophobic valine residues cause HbS molecules to line up into rigid polymers. These insoluble strands physically contort the RBC into a sickle shape.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the taut, deoxygenated state the exposed hydrophobic valine residues cause HbS molecules to line up into rigid polymers. These insoluble strands physically contort the RBC into a sickle shape.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies
questions.stem: This peripheral blood smear from a patient with G6PD deficiency shows red cells containing small dark peripheral inclusions (arrowed). What are these inclusions composed of?

explanation.summary: The inclusions are Heinz bodies, clumps of oxidatively denatured hemoglobin that attach to the inner RBC membrane. They form during oxidative stress in G6PD deficiency and are best seen with supravital stains.
explanation.whyCorrect: The inclusions are Heinz bodies, clumps of oxidatively denatured hemoglobin that attach to the inner RBC membrane. They form during oxidative stress in G6PD deficiency and are best seen with supravital stains.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies
questions.stem: This blood smear from a G6PD-deficient patient shows red cells with a scooped-out defect in their membrane (arrowed), alongside a neutrophil and normal erythrocytes. What mechanism produces this characteristic cell shape?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Osmotic swelling from excess intracellular water

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mechanical shearing of RBCs by intravascular fibrin strands

choices.label: D
choices.text: Splenic macrophages remove the membrane segment containing a Heinz body

choices.label: E
choices.text: Enzymatic digestion of the membrane by neutrophil elastase

explanation.summary: These are bite cells. As RBCs with Heinz bodies pass through the spleen, macrophages engulf and remove the portion of membrane to which the Heinz body is attached, leaving a bitten-out contour rather than destroying the whole cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: These are bite cells. As RBCs with Heinz bodies pass through the spleen, macrophages engulf and remove the portion of membrane to which the Heinz body is attached, leaving a bitten-out contour rather than destroying the whole cell.

questions.topicName: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase and Pyruvate Kinase Deficiencies
questions.stem: This labeled diagram shows the enzyme (in red) driving conversion of glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphogluconate while cycling NADP+/NADPH and oxidized/reduced glutathione. Deficiency of this enzyme most directly causes which consequence in red blood cells?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased ATP production for membrane ion pumps

explanation.summary: The diagram is the hexose monophosphate (pentose phosphate) shunt step catalyzed by G6PD, which regenerates NADPH. NADPH keeps glutathione reduced so it can detoxify peroxides; when G6PD is deficient, reduced glutathione falls and RBCs cannot neutralize oxidative stress, leading to hemolysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The diagram is the hexose monophosphate (pentose phosphate) shunt step catalyzed by G6PD, which regenerates NADPH. NADPH keeps glutathione reduced so it can detoxify peroxides; when G6PD is deficient, reduced glutathione falls and RBCs cannot neutralize oxidative stress, leading to hemolysis.

questions.stem: The rounded cells on the right of this diagram formed after partial removal of the red cell membrane. Why are these cells especially prone to hemolysis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They lack GPI-anchored complement inhibitors CD55 and CD59

choices.label: B
choices.text: They have a spectrin cytoskeletal mutation acquired in warm AHA

choices.label: C
choices.text: They have lost excess membrane and cannot deform

choices.label: D
choices.text: They contain hemoglobin S that polymerizes under low oxygen tension

choices.label: E
choices.text: They are overloaded with iron granules that damage the membrane

explanation.summary: Macrophages remove chunks of the antibody-coated membrane, leaving cells that round up. Lacking spare membrane, they cannot contort through tiny capillaries and splenic cords and are destroyed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Macrophages remove chunks of the antibody-coated membrane, leaving cells that round up. Lacking spare membrane, they cannot contort through tiny capillaries and splenic cords and are destroyed.

questions.stem: This pentameric antibody is characteristic of cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Which property allows it to cause the red cell clumping illustrated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It opsonizes cells only for splenic phagocytosis at body temperature

choices.label: B
choices.text: It inserts directly into the RBC membrane to form lytic pores

choices.label: C
choices.text: It binds the Rh D antigen with high avidity at 37 degrees C

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is warm-reactive and most active in the trunk vasculature

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its ten antigen-binding sites let a single molecule bridge multiple RBCs

explanation.summary: As a pentamer with ten binding sites, this antibody cross-links several red cells at once, forming the agglutinates typical of cold AHA when blood cools.
explanation.whyCorrect: As a pentamer with ten binding sites, this antibody cross-links several red cells at once, forming the agglutinates typical of cold AHA when blood cools.

questions.stem: The arrow on this peripheral blood smear points to an abnormally large, oval-shaped red blood cell among smaller normal erythrocytes. What is this cell called?

explanation.summary: The arrowed cell is a macro-ovalocyte, an enlarged oval red cell characteristic of megaloblastic anemia. It results from impaired DNA synthesis in erythroid precursors, causing nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony and abnormally large red cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The arrowed cell is a macro-ovalocyte, an enlarged oval red cell characteristic of megaloblastic anemia. It results from impaired DNA synthesis in erythroid precursors, causing nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony and abnormally large red cells.

questions.stem: The central labeled white blood cell on this smear is characteristic of megaloblastic anemia. A neutrophil is considered hypersegmented when its nucleus contains more than how many lobes?

explanation.summary: Hypersegmented neutrophils have nuclei with more than five lobes and are a hallmark of megaloblastic anemia due to impaired DNA synthesis in myeloid precursors. They appear alongside macro-ovalocytes on the peripheral smear.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hypersegmented neutrophils have nuclei with more than five lobes and are a hallmark of megaloblastic anemia due to impaired DNA synthesis in myeloid precursors. They appear alongside macro-ovalocytes on the peripheral smear.

questions.stem: This schematic shows the metabolic pathway leading from fatty acids and branched-chain amino acids to myelin. The enzyme converting methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA requires a cofactor; when that cofactor is deficient, which substance accumulates and can be measured in serum to confirm the deficiency?

explanation.summary: The reaction converting methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA is catalyzed by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which uses vitamin B12 as a cofactor. In B12 deficiency this step is blocked, methylmalonyl-CoA accumulates, and elevated serum methylmalonic acid results, impairing myelin synthesis and producing neurologic deficits.
explanation.whyCorrect: The reaction converting methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA is catalyzed by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which uses vitamin B12 as a cofactor. In B12 deficiency this step is blocked, methylmalonyl-CoA accumulates, and elevated serum methylmalonic acid results, impairing myelin synthesis and producing neurologic deficits.
